did_you_know.text: Did you know? The chapter opens with two rhetorical questions: Why are the nations in turmoil, and why do the peoples devise futile plans? From the very beginning, this highlights the contrast between human unrest and the pointlessness of their schemes.

Did you know? This verse describes the kings of the earth and the rulers gathering together, but their purpose is to act against the LORD and His Anointed—that is, against the LORD and His chosen king.
Did you know? The rebels use images of chains and ropes: they want to break free and throw off what they see as restraints and authority.

Did you know? The LORD’s response to these schemes is portrayed vividly: the One seated in heaven laughs and mocks them. The contrast between the turmoil on earth and the calm position in heaven is especially striking.

Did you know? In contrast to the gathering of the kings in the preceding verses, there is now a proclamation that a king has been appointed on Zion, God’s holy mountain. Zion is thus presented as the central place of this kingdom.

Did you know? The king says that he is about to proclaim a decree, and within his words comes the declaration, “You are my son.” The verse portrays the relationship between the LORD and the king in terms of a son and a father.
Did you know? The promise to the king is described on a worldwide scale: the nations are given to him as an inheritance, and his possession extends to “the ends of the earth.”
Did you know? The king’s power is described with two powerful images: an iron scepter and pottery shattered to pieces. Both images emphasize his strength over those who oppose him.

Did you know? In the final part of the chapter, the direction changes: after describing rebellion and punishment, it gives a direct call to the kings and judges of the earth to gain understanding and accept instruction.
Did you know? The chapter connects reverence with joy: people are called to serve the LORD with reverence, but also to rejoice—even when their joy is accompanied by trembling.
Did you know? The final verse combines warning and blessing: it warns of the LORD’s anger and the danger of perishing along the way, while declaring the happiness of all who take refuge in Him.
